messages.body_plain:

A solution to this problem would help consolidating the output data of brms when the models are fitted on multiple processors on an HPC cluster.

messages.subject_clean: Using group-level parameters as predictors
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I was hoping to be able to use the group-level estimates of a parameter from the model of one variable as predictors in the model of a second variable. This seems to have some relation to the idea of using variables without measurement error (i.e., the `se` function) but with the added bonus (?) that the predictor is shrunk a bit toward the population mean.

I'm envisioning something like:

```
m1 <- brm(y1 ~ 1 + x1 + (1 + x1 | g))
m2 <- brm(y2 ~ 1 + bx1 + (1 | g))
```

Where bx1 is the vector of per-group parameters for the relation between y1 and x1.

Thanks for your help, and thanks for pardoning my somewhat noob-ish phrasing of the question.

~J

messages.body_plain:
Hi John,

this is certainly possible in a two-step approach you seem to have in mind. Consider the following sample code:

```R

m1 <- brm(y1 ~ 1 + x1 + (1 + x1 | g))

bx1 <- coef(m1)$g[, "Estimate", "x1"]
# or ranef instead of coef to get the centered estimates
<put bx1 into your data.frame>

m2 <- brm(y2 ~ 1 + bx1 + (1 | g))
```

If you want to include the measurement / estimation error in bx1, add:

```R
sdbx1 <- coef(m1)$g[, "Est.Error", "x1"]
<put sdbx1 into your data.frame>
m2 <- brm(y2 ~ 1 + me(bx1, sdbx1) + (1 | g))
```

All the best,
Paul

messages.body_plain:
My choice to use 3 DF as the default has nothing to do with the size of your data on you don't need to change it based on this.

The reason I am using 3 DF is because I want the tail of the prior to be reasonably wide (in partricular wider than the tails of the normal distribution), while not running into sampling problems at the same time: A t distribution with 1 or 2 DFs might sometimes lead to problems in sampling because it is too wide. Hence the choice of DF = 3.

messages.body_plain:
It seems to be as if the model is heavily over-parameterized. Each combination of A, B, C, and D only have 2 observations per person. As you model (1+ A * B * C* D | subj), you have 36 parameters per person, each being barely identified by the 72 observations per person. Now consider that you have 36 random effects SD parameters as well as 36 * 35 / 2 = 630 random correlation parameters, all that with just 1440 observations in total. That's a lot.

You need stronger priors to get this to sample at all. The default priors for random effects are stronger in rstanarm than in brms, which is the reason the former is more willing to sample from your model, but still this is not a model I would recommend fitting with that few data.

That said, you can get this model to sample in brms, by adding a stronger prior on the random effects SDs, for instance

set_prior("student_t(3, 0, 2)", class = "sd")

You can also try setting inits = 0. Sometimes this helps.

Thanks Paul, that's really useful.

As you suggest, adding more data points and a tighter prior on the sd parameter resolved the issue.

Out of curiosity, my expectation was that the model would either not initialize, or return samples, even if the model is poorly identified. sigma1 <- 1.5

Sigma
b0 <- -2
exp(b0)/(1 + exp(b0))
N <- 100

p <- exp(b0 + e.vill)/(1 + exp(b0 + e.vill))
examined <- sample(seq(50:300), size = N, replace = T)
y1 <- rbinom(n = N, size = examined, prob = p[,1])
y2 <- rbinom(n = N, size = examined, prob = p[,2])
dat <- data.frame(y1, y2, n1 = examined, n2 = examined)

y1_f <- bf(y1 | trials(n1) ~ 0 + intercept)
y2_f <- bf(y2 | trials(n2) ~ 0 + intercept)
f <- mvbf(y1_f, y2_f)

fit <- brm(
  formula = f,
  family = binomial,
  data = dat, chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 194838
)

1.

brms cannot yet handle missing values on the fly, but it is on my ToDo list (see https://github.com/paul-buerkner/brms/issues/27).

y1_f <- bf(y1 | trials(n1) ~ (1 | p | group))
y2_f <- bf(y2 | trials(n2) ~ (1 | p | group))

I call this "ID-syntax". The symbol "p" is arbitrary. You can also use something else. See also ?bf and vignette("brms_multilevel")

I may have found another issue with how one of the brms ordinal functions is being processed. I'm relying heavily on your package for actual predictions (thank you!) rather than pure science so the coefficient values mean a lot to me, and some of these don't seem to make sense.

The model: I wanted to predict risk status based on a person's severity on various dimensional measures of psychosis. My model call looked like this:

gm.varyslope.ord  <- brm(as.ordered(Status) ~ severity + (1 + severity |psychosis_dimension),
                            data = dt.long,
                            iter=4000,
                            cores=4, chains=4, control = list(adapt_delta = .99), family="cumulative")

The problem: unless I'm misinterpreting, the "coef" function seems to give estimates that don't conform to the output of the "summary" function.

Is it possible that the 'coef' call is pulling the centered values for the intercepts or something, rather than the actual values?

Thank you so much! You've written an amazing package.

I am learning how to estimate non-linear models using brms.

  "N" = 27,

nlm = nls(Y ~ alpha - beta * lambda^x, data=dat,
           start=list(alpha=1, beta=1, lambda=0.9))
summary(nlm)

prior1 <- c(prior(normal(0.0, 100), nlpar = 'alpha'),
            prior(normal(0.0, 0.5), nlpar = 'lambda'),
            prior(normal(0.0, 100), nlpar = 'beta'))

fit <- brm(bf(Y ~ alpha - beta * pow(lambda, x),
               alpha + beta ~ 1, lambda ~ 1,
               nl = TRUE),
            data = dat, prior = prior1)

Any help will be appreciated.
Thanks!

  real sigma;
  sigma <- 1 / sqrt(tau);
}
model {
  real m[N];
  for (i in 1:N)
    m[i] <- alpha - beta * pow(lambda, x[i]);

  Y ~ normal(m, sigma);

  beta ~ normal(0.0, 1000);
  lambda ~ uniform(.5, 1);
  tau ~ gamma(.0001, .0001);
}
generated quantities{
  real Y_mean[N];
  real Y_pred[N];
  for(i in 1:N){
    # Posterior parameter distribution of the mean
    Y_mean[i] <- alpha - beta * pow(lambda, x[i]);
    # Posterior predictive distribution
    Y_pred[i] <- normal_rng(Y_mean[i], sigma);
}
}
"

messages.subject: Question about setting up `hypothesis`
messages.subject_clean: Question about setting up `hypothesis`
messages.body_plain:
I'm looking for help interpreting the hypothesis function. Say I have a model with two factors, A and B, and a grouping variable (where only a random intercept is to be estimated for the grouping variable). The first factor has three levels, A1, A2, and A3, whereas factor B has 2: B1 and B2. I set up a model with something like

fit <- brm(y ~ A*B + (1 | group), data=dat)

If I want to look at evidence for the directional hypothesis that A2 is lower than A1 at the level of B1, Is it true that the call is as simple as

hypothesis(fit, "A2 < A1")

Then, if I wanted to look at evidence for the directional hypothesis that A2 is lower than A1 at the level of B2, the call just needs to include the relevant interaction on each side:

hypothesis(fit, "A2 + A2:B2 < A1 + A1:B2")

Second, to what extent does the result of that first hypothesis (however it should be specified) compare to running a separate model with levels A1 and A2 collapsed as a single factor and then comparing the two models with WAIC or LOO? Are there situations with models this simple where it would still be expected that the evidence ratio and WAIC/LOO will give different results?

Thanks,
Patrick

messages.body_plain:
Ah, sometimes airing a question helps with at least part of answering it.

The first hypothesis, is A2 < A1 at B1, should instead be

hypothesis(fit, "A2 < Intercept")

given that in this case (I think?) the effect of A1 at B1 is the Intercept term.

Second, the WAIC/LOO is definitely not the right way to go as an alternative to this hypothesis. Collapsing A2 into A1 disallows an effect of A2 at either B1 or B2, so collapsing isn't a good stand-in for asking about what happens just when B = B1. Is there a different way to construct the formula so as to test this hypothesis through WAIC/LOO model comparison?

messages.body_plain:
The correct way of specifying such hypothesis depends on the coding of the factors. If both A and B are dummy coded (default) with reference category 1, than
A1 vs A2 at B1 should just be "A2 < 0", since the coefficient A2 ist the difference between A2 and the reference (A1) at the reference of all other factors (B1).

The point with LOO and WAIC is actually somewhat different, since you are asking a completely different question, that is "which model provides better out-of-sample predictions?.
Even if you completely collapsed A1 and A2, this might not decrease model fit, since the true difference of A1 and A2 might (for instance) just go into the random intercept if there is no variation of A within each group (i.e. only a certain A level per group).

Hi Paul,
     Okay, but now I'm worried that I'm misunderstanding something critical because I'm pretty confused by what the marginal_effects plots are showing me in relation to hypothesis. To give a bit more context, I'm doing a bit of exploration with quantile regression, using family = asym_laplace and setting quantile=0.2. In the data I'm working with, the factor A is called "Condition" and can take values of "Not Studied", "CFS", or "Binocular." Factor B is called "cue_correct_fct," and it can take values of "0" or "1". "Not Studied" and "0" are the reference categories, as indicated by

> levels(d$Condition)
[1] "Not Studied" "CFS"         "Binocular"

> levels(d$cue_correct_fct)
[1] "0" "1"

It seems to be the case that A2 (ConditionCFS) is less than A1 at B1 based on

> hypothesis(fit, "ConditionCFS < 0")
Hypothesis Tests for class b:
                   Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Evid.Ratio Star
(ConditionCFS) < 0    -0.09      0.01     -Inf    -0.06        Inf    *
---
'*': The expected value under the hypothesis lies outside the 95% CI.

So, I thought I would interpret that as evidence for the conclusion that the first quintile in ConditionCFS is lower than the first quintile of the reference Condition (Not Studied) at cue_correct_fct=0.

But when I look at the marginal effects with

> marginal_effects(fit, effects = "Condition:cue_correct_fct")

I don't see how to relate that figure with the results of the hypothesis. I would have thought that either the evidence ratio would be lower in the hypothesis or that there would be a greater distance between the credible intervals of the Not Studied and CFS condition at cue_correct_fct=0. Why isn't that the case?

Thanks for your time,
Patrick

messages.body_plain:
None overlapping CIs (or CIs that don't overlap the estimate of the other group) are just rough proxys of significance, because they don't take correlations between parameters into account.

So, the results of hypothesis and marginal_effects are not opposed to each other. When it comes to testing differences, you need to trust hypothesis.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have a question about the meta-analysis model in brms. These are models of the form
yi | se(sei) ~

It is my understanding we are using this to fit this mathematical model. Let yi be the effect sizes and sei be the standard errors of the effect size.

Then we assume
yi ~ normal(theta_i, sei^2)

where theta_i is study's "actual" effect size. Then
theta_i ~ normal(mu, tau^2)

 And mu and sigma have priors, maybe something like
mu ~ normal(0, 10)
tau ~ cauchy(0, 3)

This mathematical model is described here, with Stan code: http://mc-stan.org/users/documentation/case-studies/divergences_and_bias.html

So here is a real example. You can find the data set in this github repo <https://github.com/tmastny/periodization-meta-analysis/blob/master/factorized_periodization.csv>, but any data should work.

m <- brm(effect_size | se(standard_error) ~ 1 + (1 | study), data = d)

But how do I sample the tau parameter of this model?

If I call
posterior_summary(m)
I don't see any parameter that looks like the tau in the mathematical model.

What am I missing?

I've also tried
se(standard_error, sigma = TRUE)
but I don't think that is what I want. For example, in the Stan code of the model with sigma true, I see
normal_lpdf(Y[n] | mu[n], sqrt(sigma^2 + se2[n]))
which doesn't seem like what I want.

Maybe this what I'm looking for, but I'm not familiar with that parameterization. And if this is what I want, why is sigma=TRUE not the default (like it is in the Stan 8 schools model linked above)? It was briefly discussed here, https://github.com/paul-buerkner/brms/issues/114 but I'd be interested in the background.

Thanks,

Tim

sd__study__Intercept is tau.

The reason sigma is set to FALSE by default in se has to reasons: First (and most importantly) it ensure backwards compatibility. Second, estimating tau via a random effect instead of directly via sigma is in line with how other packages handle it and also allows for better plotting of study effects.
